<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{DEF: quasi idempotent}
Let $R$ be a ring, an element $e \in R$ is said to be a quasi-idempotent element of $R$ if $e^2=ke$ where $k$  is a central unit in $R$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{remark on anti-commutator}
    It is clear that every idempotent element is a quasi idempotent element with $k=1.$ The trivial idempotents $0,1$ are also trivial quasi-idempotents in the ring $R$.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- eg-1: body_md -->
Let $R$ be a ring and $e$ be an idempotent in $R$. Also let $k$ be a central unit in $R$ such that $e\neq ke$. Then, $x=ek$ is a quasi-idmpotent which is not an idempotent.
<!-- end eg-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
A ring $R$ is said to be reversible if for every $a,b \in R$ such that $ab=0$ implies $ba=0$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{Char of rev rings}\cite[Proposition 1.4.]{Jung2015}
    A ring $R$ is reversible if and only if for every $a,b \in R$ such that $ab$ is an idempotent implies that $ba$ is also an idempotent.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{main 1}
    A ring $R$ is reversible if and only if for every $a,b \in R$ such that $ab$ is a quasi-idempotent implies that $ba$ is also a quasi-idempotent.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Suppose that $R$ is a reversible ring and let $a,b \in R$ such that $ab$ is a quasi-idempotent element in $R$. Therefore, we have the following equations:
\begin{align*}
    &(ab)^2=k( ab) \text{ for some central unit } k \in R.\\
    &\implies ab(ab-k)=0.
\end{align*}
Using the fact that $R$ is reversible, we get $b(ab-k)a=0$ which can be further reduced to $baba-bka=0.$ Now we use the fact that the element $k$ is central in $R$ and hence $baba-kba=0$. This is exactly $(ba)^2=k(ba)$ and hence, $ba$ is a quasi-idempotent as required.
Conversely, suppose that the ring $R$ satisfies the property that for every $a,b \in R$ such that $ab$ is a quasi-idempotent implies that $ba$ is also a quasi-idempotent. Now consider $a,b\in R$ such that $ab=0$. Since $ab=0$ it is trivially a quasi-idempotent (see \ref{remark on anti-commutator}). Therefore, $ba$ is also a quasi-idempotent by our hypothesis. Hence, there exists a central unit $k \in R$ such that $(ba)^2=k(ba)$. However since $ab=0$, this reduces to $0=(ba)^2=k(ba)$. Hence $k(ba)=0$ gives $ba=0$ since $k$ is a unit in $R$. Therefore the ring $R$ is reversible as desired.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
A ring $R$ is i-reversible if for every $a,b \in R$ such that $ab$ is a non-zero idempotent implies that $ba$ is also an idempotent.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{main 2}
    A ring $R$ is i-reversible if and only if for every $a,b \in R$ such that $ab$ is a non-zero quasi-idempotent implies that $ba$ is also an quasi-idempotent.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Suppose that $R$ is an i-reversible ring and let $a,b \in R$ such that $ab$ is a non-zero quasi-idempotent. This gives that $(ab)^2=k(ab)$ for some central unit $k \in R$. Set $a'=k^{-1}a\in R$ and consider the following equalities:
\begin{align*}
    (a'b)^2&=(k^{-1})^2(ab)^2\\
    &=(k^{-1})^2(kab)\\
    &=k^{-1}ab\\
    &=ab.
\end{align*}
Therefore, $a'b$ is an idempotent in $R$. Also, $a'b=k^{-1}ab$ is a non-zero idempotent in $R$ for if otherwise, $ab=0$ which is not true due to our hypothesis. Therefore, using the fact that our ring $R$ is an i-reversible ring, we have that $(ba')^2=ba$ which gives rise to the following equalities:
\begin{align*}
    (ba')^2=&( ba')\\
    \implies (bk^{-1}a)^2=& \ bk^{-1}a\\
    \implies k^{-1}(ba)^2=& \ ba
\end{align*}
This finally gives $(ba)^2=k(ba)$as required. Conversely, suppose that the ring $R$ satisfies the property that for every $a,b \in R$ such that $ab$ is a non-zero quasi-idempotent implies that $ba$ is also an quasi-idempotent. Consider $a,b \in R$ such that $ab$ is a non-zero idempotent. Since $ab$ is a non-zero idempotent, by Remark \ref{remark on anti-commutator} $ab$ is also a non-zero quasi-idempotent. Therefore, $(ba)^2=k(ba)$ for some central unit $k\in R.$ Now consider the following expression for the element $(ba)^3 \in R:$
\begin{align*}
    (ba)^3&=b(ab)^2a\\
    &=b(ab)a\\
    &=(ba)^2\\
    &=k^2(ba).
\end{align*}
On the other hand, we also have that $(ba)^3=(ba)(ba)^2=(ba)(k(ba))=k(ba)^2=k^2(ba).$ Combining the two equalities for the element $(ba)^3$ we get $k^2(ba)=k(ba)$ which reduces to $kba=ba$. Since $(ba)^2=kba$, we finally get $(ba)^2=ba$ thereby completing the proof.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
A ring $R$ is called a semi-commutative ring if for every $a,b \in R$ such that $ab=0$, we have $aRb=0$.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{main 3}
  A ring $R$  is semi-commutative if and only if for every $a,b \in R$ such that $ab$ is a quasi-idempotent with $(ab)^2=k(ab)$ for some central unit $k \in R$, we have that $(k-ab)aRb(k-ab)=0.$
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Suppose that $R$ is semi-commutative and let $a,b \in R$ such that $(ab)^2=k(ab)$ for some central unit $k \in R.$ This automatically gives $(k-ab)ab=0$. Using the semi-commutative property of $R$ we get $(k-ab)aRb=0$ and hence $(k-ab)aRb(k-ab)=0.$ Conversely, suppose that $ab=0$ then $(ab)^2=k(ab)$ for any non trivial central idempotent $k\in R$. We pick any such central unit $k$ and by our hypothesis we get $kaRbk=0$ but since $k$ is a unit in $R$, this reduces to $aRb=0$. Therefore $R$ is semi-commutative.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
\cite[Theorem 1.]{SaadZailaee2026}
    A ring $R$  is semi-commutative if and only if for every $a,b \in R$ such that $ab$ is an idempotent, we have that $(k-ab)aRb(k-ab)=0.$
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
The proof is direct by setting $k=1$ in the proof of \Cref{main 3}.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
A ring $R$ is called an i-domain if for every idempotent $ab \in R$ for some $a,b \in R$ we have either $a\in I(b)$ or $b \in I(a)$ where $I(a) $ and $I(b)$ represent the two sided ideals generated by $a$ and $b $ respectively.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
A ring $R$ is an i-domain if and only if for every quasi-idempotent $ab \in R$ for some $a,b \in R$ we have either $a\in I(b)$ or $b \in I(a)$.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Suppose that $ab$ is a quasi-idempotent elements in $R$. There exists a central unit $k \in R$ such that $(ab)^2=kab$, we have that $(a'b)$ is an idempotent element, where $a'=k^{-1}a$. Using the fact that $R$ is an i-domain, either $a'\in I(b)$ or $b \in I(a')$ which in turn implies that either $a\in I(b)$ or $b \in I(a)$.
     The converse is obvious, considering the fact that every idempotent is a quasi-idempotent.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
